questions.text: Arrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph: (P) It was a cold winter morning. (Q) She decided to brew a hot cup of tea. (R) The wind howled outside the window. (S) The warmth of the mug comforted her instantly.
questions.explanation: Logical flow: P sets the scene (cold morning), R adds atmospheric detail (howling wind), Q shows her response to the cold (brewing tea), S gives the outcome (warmth/comfort). P→R→Q→S is the natural cause-and-effect chain.

questions.text: Arrange: (P) Exercise also improves mental health by releasing endorphins. (Q) A sedentary lifestyle is one of the leading causes of chronic disease. (R) Regular physical activity reduces the risk of heart disease, diabetes, and obesity. (S) Despite knowing these benefits, most people fail to exercise regularly.

options.text: Q-R-P-S (problem → physical benefits → mental benefits → irony)

questions.explanation: Q introduces the problem (sedentary lifestyle = disease risk). R states the direct solution/benefit (exercise reduces disease). P adds another benefit (mental health/endorphins). S provides the ironic twist — despite benefits, people still don't exercise. This Q→R→P→S order follows problem → evidence → elaboration → contrast.

questions.text: Arrange: (P) The committee reviewed its findings before publishing the report. (Q) Several inconsistencies were found in the preliminary data. (R) An independent audit was commissioned to verify the results. (S) Only after the audit was the final report released to the public.
questions.explanation: P: committee reviews data. Q: inconsistencies found (consequence of review). R: audit commissioned (response to inconsistencies). S: final publication after audit. P→Q→R→S is strictly chronological and causal. Option B (Q before P) is tempting — inconsistencies could come first — but P ('reviewed before publishing') sets the stage for what was found.

questions.text: Arrange: (P) This made the discovery all the more remarkable. (Q) Alexander Fleming noticed an unusual mould growing on a petri dish. (R) He observed that the mould appeared to be killing the surrounding bacteria. (S) The mould had been left there by accident.
questions.explanation: Q: Fleming notices the mould (initial observation). S: explains it was there by accident (background context, why it was notable). R: key discovery — mould killing bacteria. P: 'all the more remarkable' = concluding emphasis, referencing the accidental nature of the discovery. Q→S→R→P is the natural narrative arc.

questions.text: Arrange: (P) However, critics argue that technology has also deepened inequality between those with and without access. (Q) The digital revolution has transformed communication, commerce, and education worldwide. (R) Proponents point to falling costs and rising smartphone penetration as evidence of democratisation. (S) The debate reflects a broader tension between technological optimism and structural realism.
questions.explanation: Q makes the broad claim (digital revolution transformed the world). R supports it (proponents: costs falling, smartphones spreading). P introduces the counterargument (but critics say inequality deepened). S synthesises both sides (tension between optimism and realism). Q→R→P→S follows the standard argumentative structure: claim → support → counter → synthesis.

questions.text: Arrange: (P) These neurons form the biological basis of what psychologists call 'emotional contagion'. (Q) When we observe someone experiencing pain, mirror neurons in our brain activate as if we felt the pain ourselves. (R) This automatic neural response explains why watching someone cry often makes us feel sad too. (S) Mirror neurons were discovered in the 1990s while studying macaque monkeys.
questions.explanation: S introduces mirror neurons (historical discovery, 1990s monkeys). Q explains the mechanism (pain observation → self-activation). P names the phenomenon (emotional contagion). R gives a real-world application (watching someone cry → feeling sad). S→Q→P→R follows discovery → mechanism → concept name → example, the classic science explanation arc.

questions.text: Arrange: (P) The paradox is that language, our primary tool for self-expression, is fundamentally a shared and public system. (Q) Every act of self-expression is therefore simultaneously an act of conformity to pre-existing linguistic structures. (R) When we speak, we do not invent the words or grammar — we inherit them from our community. (S) Yet we insist that our words are uniquely and authentically our own.
questions.explanation: P states the central paradox (language = shared yet used for self-expression). R explains it (we inherit words/grammar, don't invent them). S introduces the tension/irony ('yet we insist our words are our own'). Q draws the philosophical implication from S (every self-expression = conformity). P→R→S→Q builds the argument: paradox → evidence → ironic observation → conclusion.
